ABSTRACT: Driven by the rapid development of 5G/6G
communications, high-performance computing, and artificial in-
telligence, the metallization of high-aspect-ratio through-holes
(THs) in printed circuit boards (PCBs) imposes stringent
requirements on the thickness uniformity and interconnect
reliability of electroplated copper layers. This study systematically
investigates the application of a novel leveler, thiazolyl blue (MTT),
for PCB THs’ electroplating, successfully realizing high-quality
conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio (10:1) THs. Electro-
chemical analyses demonstrate that MTT significantly enhances the
cathodic polarization and efectively inhibits the reduction of Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterizations confirm

signal integrity, current-carrying capacity, and long-term

However, during the practical electroplating of high-aspect
ratio THs, the initial current distribution is highly nonuniform
due to geometric constraints. The local current density at the
via opening is significantly higher than that at the center,
accompanied by severe mass transfer limitations of Cu<sup>2+</sup> within
the hole. This multiphysics imbalance frequently triggers the
“dog-bone” defect, characterized by excessive copper accumu-
lation at the via opening and excessively thin deposits on the
inner walls.<sup>11</sup> Such nonuniform deposition severely compro-
mises the electrical and mechanical performance of the
interconnected structures, constituting a universal bottleneck
in the high-density interconnect (HDI) industry.<sup>12</sup> To
overcome this challenge, it is imperative to introduce
suppressors, accelerators, and levelers into the acidic copper
sulfate bath.<sup>13</sup> The precise synergistic and competitive
adsorption among these three additives dynamically modulates
the deposition kinetics at diferent spatial locations within the
TH, ultimately achieving high-quality conformal interconnec-
tion.
Typically, polyether macromolecules (e.g., polyethylene
glycol, PEG) serve as suppressors; bridged by chloride ions,
they profoundly enhance cathodic polarization and retard
copper growth.<sup>14</sup> Sulfonate compounds bearing thiol or
disulfide groups (e.g., bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide, SPS) act
as accelerators: they capture Cu<sup>2+</sup> at the cathode interface and
lower the activation barrier for its reduction.<sup>15</sup> Among the
plating formulations, the leveler plays the most critica
interfacial regulatory role. By preferentially adsorbing at
strongly convected regions (e.g., the opening), the leveler
establishes a localized high-impedance barrier that inhibits
overplating,<sup>16−18</sup> thereby compelling the spatial electric field
lines to redistribute deeper into TH.<sup>19−21</sup> To date, various
commercial dyes have been reported as levelers (e.g., Janus
Green B, tetrazolium blue chloride, PAN).<sup>22−24</sup> Meanwhile,
some researchers have devoted eforts to the synthesis of nove
polymeric levelers (e.g., VIBDGE, PBDGE, Sudan-QNL).
Nevertheless, each of the aforementioned levelers exhibits
specific limitations. Polymeric levelers such as VIBDGE and
PBDGE, despite their promising performance, typically require
multistep synthesis and tedious purification procedures, which
considerably increase the production cost and hinder their
practical scalability. Commercial dye-based levelers (e.g., Janus
Green B) are readily accessible and have been widely adopted
in industry with proven efectiveness; however, as the aspec
ratio of through-holes continues to increase, further enhance
ment of throwing power remains highly desirable to ensure the
thickness uniformity and long-term reliability of the copper
interconnects. In this regard, MTT ofers a compelling
combination of advantages: it is a commercially available, of
the-shelf reagent that can be directly procured at low cost
entirely eliminating the need for custom synthesis or
purification, and as will be demonstrated in Section 3.5, it
delivers a throwing power (TP = 96.8%) that markedly
outperforms the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under
identical bath composition and process conditions. Therefore,
a systematic investigation of MTT as a tailored leveler for high
aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating is of urgent
practical significance.
It is worth noting that MTT has previously been explored in
other copper electrodeposition contexts. Ogutu et al. first
introduced MTT as a single additive for superconformal filling
of through-glass vias (TGVs) with aspect ratios up to 10:1 in
methanesulfonate-based electrolytes.<sup>28</sup> More recently, Yang et
al. compared MTT with iodonitrotetrazolium chloride (INT)
in a sulfate-based acidic electroplating system for blind via
copper filling and reported that MTT exhibits a conformal
type filling tendency rather than the bottom-up superfilling
behavior required for microvia applications.<sup>29</sup> However, the
performance of MTT in high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole
electroplating�an application scenario in which conformal,
uniform thickness distribution rather than bottom-up super
filling is the primary objective�has not yet been systematically
investigated. The present work therefore complements these
prior studies by examining MTT as a leveler within a sulfate
based acidic electroplating system specifically tailored for
through-hole plating, thereby establishing the suitability of
MTT for this distinct application scenario. It should also be
noted that our group recently reported tetrazolium blue
chloride (TB) as a leveler for copper through-hole electro
plating. Although TB and MTT both belong to the tetrazolium
family, their molecular architectures difer considerably: TB
bears two methoxy-phenyl substituents on the tetrazolium ring,
whereas MTT carries a 4,5-dimethylthiazole moiety together
with two unsubstituted phenyl groups. Such substituent
diferences lead to distinguishable electrochemical responses
and leveling outcomes. At their respective optimized
conditions, TB exhibits a relatively large convection-dependent
polarization response with Δη ≈ 31 mV, yielding a TP value of
136.7% along with preferential Cu(111) growth, whereas
MTT, as demonstrated in the present study, shows a smaller
Δη ≈ 19.3 mV and afords a TP value of 96.8% accompanied
by a preferential Cu(200) growth (see Sections 3.4 and 3.5). A
recent comparative investigation by Yang et al. likewise
reported that MTT exhibits filling characteristics distinct
from those of its nitro-substituted tetrazolium analog INT,
further supporting the notion that subtle substituent variations
within the tetrazolium family can give rise to markedly
diferent leveling behaviors.<sup>29</sup> These observations together
underscore that MTT represents a distinct leveler within the
tetrazolium family and warrants dedicated investigation for
high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating applications.
This work systematically investigates the application
performance of thiazolyl blue tetrazolium bromide (MTT) as
a highly eficient leveler in PCB TH electroplating. Utilizing
scanning electron microscopy and laser confocal microscopy,
the exceptional microscopic leveling efect of MTT on the
surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper layer is
intuitively revealed. Furthermore, X-ray difraction and contact
angle measurements are employed to deeply analyze its
regulatory efects on crystallographic phase evolution and
solid−liquid interfacial wettability. More importantly, this
study establishes a multiscale analytical framework integrating
macroscopic electrochemical analyses with microscopic
quantum chemical calculations to comprehensively elucidate
the TH filling mechanism of MTT under multiphysics
coupling. Ultimately, through precise optimization of the
additive concentration ratio and related processing parameters,
high-quality conformal electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio
PCB THs is successfully realized.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Surface Analysis of Electroplated Copper Layer

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Surface Analysis of Electroplated Copper Layer
The regulatory efect of the MTT additive on the surface
morphology of the electrodeposited copper layers was
systematically investigated utilizing a scanning electron micro-
scope and a laser confocal microscope. As depicted in Figure
^ { \mathrm { 1 b , } }
the copper coating electrodeposited in VMS (without
MTT) exhibits a distinctly rough and uneven morphology,
characterized by the presence of large and coarse crystalline
particles on the surface. In sharp contrast, upon the
introduction of MTT into the plating bath (Figure 1c−g),
the surface flatness of the coatings shows a dramatic
enhancement. With an incremental increase in MTT
concentration, the crystalline morphology transitions pro-
gressively toward a highly compact and smooth state. This
observation unambiguously indicates that MTT possesses
excellent leveling capability at the microscopic scale, efectively
refining the grain size and upgrading the surface quality. This
conclusion was further substantiated by the three-dimensional
(3D) surface topography mapping. As illustrated in Figures S1
and S2, the surface roughness of the deposited layers decreases
precipitously with elevating MTT concentrations, dropping
from 0.545 to 0.147 μm. Such a smooth surface characteristic
is highly advantageous for high-frequency signal transmission
in printed circuit boards (PCBs). During high-frequency signal
propagation, dictated by the skin efect,<sup>41</sup> the skin depth of the
alternating current becomes increasingly shallow at higher
frequencies. When the skin depth diminishes to a scale
comparable to the surface roughness of the copper traces, the
high-frequency current is forced to travel along the tortuous,
rugged surface contour, thereby substantially elongating the
actual conductive pathway. Consequently, a copper deposit
with inherently low surface roughness can substantially reduce
the transmission loss of high-frequency signals. In summary,
functioning as a highly eficient leveler, MTT can significantly
enhance the surface flatness and compactness of the electro
plated copper layers, fulfilling the stringent physical require-
ments for high-frequency interconnects.

The impact of MTT on the crystallographic structure and grain
size evolution of the electroplated copper layers was
investigated utilizing XRD. According to the XRD patterns
(Figure 4a), characteristic difraction peaks corresponding to
the (111), (200), and (220) planes of copper are distinctly
observed at 2θ values of 43.3°, 50.4°, and
, respectively.
As depicted in Figure 4a, with the incremental addition of
MTT into the plating bath, the intensity of the (111) peak
exhibits no obvious variation, whereas the (200) peak
progressively intensifies and the (220) peak gradually
attenuates. To quantitatively elucidate the regulatory efect of
MTT on the preferred crystallographic orientation, the relative
texture coeficients
( \mathrm { R T C } _ { \mathrm { ( h k l ) } } )
for the respective lattice planes
were calculated based on the following equation:
\mathrm{RTC} _ {(\mathrm{hkl})} = \frac {I _ {(\mathrm{hkl})} / I _ {0 (\mathrm{hkl})}}{\sum (I _ {(\mathrm{hkl})} / I _ {0 (\mathrm{hkl})})} \times 100\tag{4}
where
I _ { O ( \mathrm { h k l } ) }
represents the standard difraction peak intensity
of a randomly oriented copper powder sample and
I _ { \mathrm { ( h k l ) } }
denotes the measured difraction peak intensity of the actual
electrodeposited copper films. The quantitative results (Figure
4c) reveal that as the MTT concentration escalates from 0 mg/
L to 60 mg/L,
\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 2 0 0 ) }
sharply surges from 17.63% to 52.52%,
\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 1 1 1 ) }
exhibits a marginal decline, and
\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 2 2 0 ) }
plummets
dramatically from 52.12% to 24.39%. This rigorous texture
coeficient analysis unambiguously demonstrates that the
incorporation of MTT does not induce a preferred orientation
along the Cu(111) plane, but rather intensely promotes the
preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane. Furthermore, the
Scherrer equation was employed to quantitatively assess the
influence of MTT concentration on the crystalline grain size
(D) of the copper deposits:
D = \frac {K \lambda}{\beta \cos \theta}\tag{5}
where K is the Scherrer constant (assigned as 0.89), λ is the
incident X-ray wavelength (0.1541 nm), β represents the full
width at half-maximum (fwhm) of the difraction peak, and θ is
the corresponding Bragg difraction angle. The calculated
results (Figure 4b) dictate that within the concentration range
of 0−50 mg/L, the grain size is notably refined from 23.30 to
18.46 nm as the MTT concentration elevates. Nevertheless,
further exceeding this MTT concentration threshold leads to
an anomalous grain coarsening. This phenomenon indicates
that there exists an optimal concentration window for MTT,
within which the most highly eficient grain refinement can be
achieved.
Although the orientation evolution analyzed above and the
conformal filling reported in Section
are governed by
diferent proximate mechanisms�the former by the facet
selective character of MTT adsorption on the cathode and the
latter by the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA)�they
share a common origin in the surface adsorption of MTT and
concurrently emerge at the same optimum concentration (50
mg/L). The two efects are functionally complementary in the
present context: CDA establishes uniform Cu thickness from
the orifice to the via center, while the Cu(200) preferential
growth and the grain refinement to 18.46 nm provide a fine
grained, densely packed microstructure throughout the
conformal layer. The resulting deposit therefore satisfies
simultaneously the two principal requirements of PCB
through-hole metallization, namely conformal thickness
uniformity (which guarantees interconnect reliability) and
low surface roughness (which mitigates skin-efect-induced
signal losses).

Electroplated Copper Layer
The impact of MTT on the crystallographic structure and grain
size evolution of the electroplated copper layers was
investigated utilizing XRD. According to the XRD patterns

observed at 2θ values of 43.3°, 50.4°, and
, respectively.

exhibits no obvious variation, whereas the (200) peak
progressively intensifies and the (220) peak gradually
attenuates. To quantitatively elucidate the regulatory efect of

texture coeficients
( \mathrm { R T C } _ { \mathrm { ( h k l ) } } )
for the respective lattice planes

where
I _ { O ( \mathrm { h k l } ) }
represents the standard difraction peak intensity
of a randomly oriented copper powder sample and

L to 60 mg/L,
\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 2 0 0 ) }
sharply surges from 17.63% to 52.52%,
\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 1 1 1 ) }

\mathrm { R T C } _ { ( 2 2 0 ) }
plummets

4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, this study systematically investigated the
application performance and multiphysics coupling mecha-
nisms of MTT, acting as a leveler for copper electrodeposition
in PCB through-holes. Electrochemical evaluations demon
strate that MTT significantly enhances cathodic polarization
via a convection-dependent interfacial adsorption. Meanwhile,
microscopic morphological characterization confirms that
MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, significantly
reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to
0.147 μm. Such a smooth surface topography is highly
beneficial for mitigating the skin efect and lowering insertion
loss during high-frequency signal transmission. Density func-
tional theory analysis further elucidates that the microscopic
origin of this robust inhibitory behavior lies primarily in the
strong interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode, with the
bulk cation−π interaction with
{ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }
contributing as a minor
secondary efect. Phase structure and interface analysis
illustrate that an optimal MTT concentration (50 mg/L) not
only efectively refines the crystalline grain size and promotes
the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane but also
decreases the solid−liquid interfacial contact angle to
thereby fundamentally suppressing the generation of macro-
scopic morphological defects. Ultimately, in practical through-
hole electroplating applications, the competitive adsorption
among MTT, PEG, and SPS induces a spatially diferentiated
remodeling of polarization resistance. By establishing a high
impedance barrier at the forced-convection orifice region, the
inherent Ohmic potential drop within the through-holes is
efectively compensated. Driven by this multiphysical coupling
mechanism, the TP value of through-holes is substantially
elevated from 25.2% to 96.8%, markedly outperforming the
conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical
conditions, successfully achieving high-quality conformal
deposition and providing a theoretical and practical basis for
the fabrication of highly reliable, high-frequency 3D
interconnected PCB structures.
